why_companies_ask_this.title: Why Hash Maps Are The Most Tested Data Structure
why_companies_ask_this.content: Hash maps are the first tool every experienced engineer reaches for when they see a performance problem. They are what transformed search from O(n) to O(1), what makes databases fast with index structures, what powers caches, session stores, and feature flags. When Amazon runs a recommendation engine on 500 million users, they do not scan every user for every request — they hash. When Razorpay validates a payment in milliseconds, they look up account state in a hash map, not a sequential scan. Companies test hashing because it is the single biggest jump in everyday engineering — from code that works to code that scales. A candidate who reaches for a hash map when the problem demands it, and knows which of the four sub-patterns to apply, is signalling they have production engineering instincts, not just textbook knowledge.

company_specific.insight: Amazon's online assessments almost always include Two Sum or a Two Sum variant as the first problem. It is considered table stakes — you must solve it in O(n) using the complement-lookup pattern. An O(n²) solution will time out on the hidden test cases even if your logic is correct. The 5-minute solve target is Two Sum in under 5 minutes with correct complexity stated.

Google interviewers use Group Anagrams as a warm-up to test fingerprinting thinking. They then escalate: 'Can you do better than O(n·k·log k)?' (frequency key gives O(n·k)). Then: 'What if strings could contain Unicode?' (use a Map instead of a 26-element array). Each follow-up is testing whether you understand the algorithm or just memorised it.

These companies test Top K Frequent Elements specifically because their recommendation and surge-pricing systems need to identify the most-ordered items in a time window efficiently. They want to see the O(n) bucket sort, not the O(n log n) sort. If you give the sort version, they will ask: 'Can you do better?' If you give bucket sort first, you demonstrate product engineering awareness.

lessons.title: What Is A Hash Function?
lessons.objective: Understand what a hash function does, why it enables O(1) average-case lookups, and what properties a good hash function must have.
concepts: Hash function definition: maps any key to an integer index
The modulo operation to fit the index within array bounds
Determinism: same key always produces the same hash
Uniform distribution: spreading keys to minimise collisions
Avalanche effect: small input change produces large hash change
Why lookup is O(1) average but O(n) worst case
Real hash functions: djb2, MurmurHash, FNV
lessons.explanation:
A hash function takes any key — a string, an integer, an object — and converts it into an integer that serves as an index into a fixed-size array. The process: compute hash(key), then take hash(key) % array_size to get a valid index. This single operation lets you store and retrieve values in constant time, bypassing the need to search.

For a hash function to be useful it must be:
- Deterministic: same key → same index, every time
- Fast: O(key_length) to compute, not slower
- Uniform: keys spread evenly across array to minimise collisions
- Avalanche: changing one character completely changes the output hash, preventing clustering

The O(1) guarantee is an average-case claim, not worst-case. In the worst case, every key hashes to the same index and all operations degrade to O(n). With a good hash function and reasonably sized array, collisions are rare and the average is effectively O(1).
lessons.analogy: A hash function is a librarian with a specific rule for deciding which shelf any book goes on, based only on the book's title. You hand them any title and they immediately tell you the shelf number without searching. The rule must be consistent (same title → same shelf), fast to apply, and must spread books evenly so no shelf becomes overcrowded. A bad rule that puts everything on shelf 3 makes every lookup a shelf-3 search — O(n).

visual_explanation.description: Draw three boxes connected by arrows. Box 1 (left): 'Keys' — show 'apple', 'banana', 'cherry'. Middle arrow labelled 'hash(key) % array_size'. Box 2 (middle): 'Hash Array' — draw a vertical array of 10 slots (0-9) with some slots populated. Box 3 (right): 'Values' — show the values stored. Draw 'apple' → hash → slot 3 → 42. Draw 'banana' → hash → slot 7 → 85. Draw 'cherry' → hash → slot 3 → COLLISION with apple, showing the chaining bucket extending. Add annotation: 'O(1) average when slots are spread. O(n) worst when all keys land in one slot.'

code_example.explanation: The multiplier 31 appears in Java's String.hashCode() and is one of the most widely used hash multipliers in production. It is prime (reducing collision patterns) and multiplication by 31 can be optimised to a bit shift (31*x = (x<<5) - x), making it fast even in performance-critical code.

common_mistakes: Thinking O(1) hash map lookup is guaranteed in all cases — it is an average-case claim. A poor hash function or adversarial inputs that force all keys to the same bucket degrade every operation to O(n)

Using mutable objects or arrays as hash map keys in JavaScript — object identity (reference) is used for hashing, so two separate arrays [1,2] and [1,2] hash to different slots even though they look equal. Always use primitive keys (strings, numbers) or serialise complex keys
Not understanding why array size matters — a very small array means many collisions regardless of hash quality. Most implementations auto-resize when load factor (items/capacity) exceeds ~0.75

interview_war_story.story: The interviewer asked: 'How does a hash map work internally?' The first candidate said 'It gives O(1) lookup.' Full stop. The interviewer said 'But how?' The candidate had no answer. The second candidate said: 'A hash function converts the key to an integer via modulo array_size — that is the index. On lookup, we compute the same hash and go directly to that index. Collisions happen when two keys land at the same index — handled by chaining (linked list at each slot) or open addressing (probe for next empty slot). When too many collisions occur the table resizes and rehashes — amortized O(1) across all operations, O(n) worst case for a single resize.' The second candidate got the offer.
interview_war_story.lesson: Every engineer who has used a hash map can say 'O(1) lookup.' The interview question is whether you understand WHY. The answer is: hash function → array index → O(1) direct access. Knowing this makes you credible when discussing performance under adversarial conditions.

lessons.interview_relevance: Interviewers at every level ask 'How does a hash map work internally?' The answer that earns full marks: hash function converts key to index via modulo, collisions handled by chaining or open addressing, amortized O(1) operations with occasional O(n) resize. This lesson gives you that complete answer.

questions.question: A hash function maps the key 'apple' to index 3. The same hash function is called again with 'apple'. What index does it return?
options: A random index — hash functions are random by design
3 — hash functions must be deterministic: same input always produces same output
It depends on how many items are in the map
The next available empty slot
questions.explanation: Determinism is the most critical property of a hash function. The same key must always produce the same hash value — otherwise lookup would return the wrong slot or miss entirely. A random function would be useless as a lookup mechanism.

questions.question: A hash map has 1,000 slots and 900 stored items. Every lookup now takes O(n). What most likely caused this?
options: The hash map ran out of memory
The load factor is too high — too many items per slot — causing long collision chains that degrade lookup to O(n)
The hash function became too slow with many items
JavaScript maps automatically become O(n) above 900 items
questions.explanation: Load factor = items / capacity = 900/1000 = 0.9. Most implementations resize at 0.75. At 0.9 load, each slot has on average 0.9 items, but with clustering some slots have many more, causing long chains. The fix: resize to a larger array and rehash all items, reducing the load factor and restoring O(1) average lookups.

questions.question: Why does a good hash function use a prime number multiplier (like 31) rather than a round number (like 32)?
options: Prime numbers are faster to compute
Prime multipliers break periodic bit patterns that occur with power-of-2 multipliers, producing better distribution of hash values across the array
32 would cause overflow errors
Hash functions must always use odd numbers
questions.explanation: Power-of-2 multipliers (like 32 = 2^5) cause the lower bits of the hash to repeat in periodic patterns — this creates clusters of keys landing at the same index. Prime multipliers break this periodicity, distributing keys more uniformly. This is why 31 is used in Java's String.hashCode() — it is prime AND can be computed as (x<<5)-x for performance.

coding_quest.title: Build And Test A Hash Function
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement simpleHash(key, arraySize) using the prime-31 multiplier. Then test it: hash 10 keys ('a' through 'j') with arraySize=10 and count collisions. Then test the same 10 keys with arraySize=13 (prime). Count collisions for each. Verify that prime array sizes generally produce fewer collisions.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: A common wrong hash function uses addition instead of the polynomial multiplier: hash = (hash + charCode) % arraySize. This produces terrible distribution because 'abc' and 'bca' and 'cab' all have the same sum and hash to the same slot. The polynomial multiplier (×31) makes position matter — 'abc' and 'bca' produce different hashes.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: Logically incorrect — produces identical hashes for all anagrams of the same string, causing O(n) worst-case lookups on any dataset with words sharing the same letters

optimal_solution.complexity: O(k) per hash call where k = key length. O(n·k) to hash n keys of average length k.

test_cases.label: Avalanche: one char change = different hash
Prime size 13 has fewer collisions than size 10

hints.text: Inside the loop: take the current hash, multiply by 31, add the character code of key[i], then take modulo arraySize. This is: hash = (hash * 31 + key.charCodeAt(i)) % arraySize.

For countCollisions: loop through all keys, compute each slot using simpleHash. Store slot counts in a Map. Then count how many extra items went into already-occupied slots. If a slot has count 3, it contributes 2 collisions (the 2nd and 3rd items that collided).
Hash: for (let i = 0; i < key.length; i++) { hash = (hash * 31 + key.charCodeAt(i)) % arraySize; }. Collisions: for (const count of slots.values()) { if (count > 1) collisions += count - 1; }

lessons.mini_challenge: Implement simpleHash and test it on 10 keys ('a' through 'j') with arraySize=10 and arraySize=13. Count collisions for each. Observe that the prime size produces fewer collisions and explain why in one sentence.

theory_mcq.question: What is the basic two-step process a hash map uses to convert a key into a valid array index?
options: Sort all keys, then assign indices in sorted order
Compute hash(key) to get an integer, then take hash(key) % array_size to map that integer into a valid index range for the underlying array
Search the array linearly for an empty slot
Use the key's memory address directly as the index
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson states this exact two-step process: hash(key) produces an arbitrary integer, and the modulo operation (% array_size) constrains it to a valid index within the array's bounds — this combination is what enables O(1) average-case access.

theory_mcq.question: Why must a good hash function be 'deterministic'?
options: Determinism is optional and only improves performance slightly

If the same key produced different hash values on different calls, you could never reliably find a previously-stored value again, since a lookup needs to recompute the same index that was used during insertion
Determinism only matters for string keys, not numeric keys
Non-deterministic hash functions are actually faster
theory_mcq.explanation: Determinism is foundational, not optional: the entire hash map mechanism depends on being able to recompute the SAME index for a key during lookup as was used during insertion — without this guarantee, stored values would become unfindable.

theory_mcq.question: What does the 'avalanche effect' mean for a hash function, and why does it matter?
options: It means the hash function crashes on large inputs

A small change to the input (e.g., one character) should produce a large, seemingly unrelated change in the output hash — this prevents similar keys from clustering at nearby indices, which would otherwise increase collisions
It means hash computation gets progressively slower with each call
It refers to the hash table physically running out of memory
theory_mcq.explanation: The avalanche effect ensures similar inputs ('hello' vs 'hellp') don't produce similar (nearby) hash outputs, which would otherwise cause many similar keys to cluster in the same region of the array, increasing collisions and degrading performance.

theory_mcq.question: Why is the O(1) lookup guarantee for hash maps described as an 'average-case' claim rather than a worst-case guarantee?
options: Because hash maps are always O(1) no matter what

Because in the worst case, all keys could hash to the SAME index, causing every operation to degrade to O(n) as the lookup must scan through all colliding entries — good hash functions and reasonable array sizing make this rare in practice, but the worst case is still mathematically possible
Because O(1) is just a marketing term with no technical meaning
Because average-case and worst-case are identical concepts
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson is explicit: 'the O(1) guarantee is an average-case claim, not worst-case... in the worst case, every key hashes to the same index and all operations degrade to O(n).' This distinction matters for rigorous interview reasoning about complexity.

logic_mcq.question: Given `simpleHash(key, arraySize)` is called twice with the exact same key and arraySize, what must be true of the two return values, based on the determinism property?
options: They could be different each time, since hashing involves randomness
They must be IDENTICAL every time — this is the defining guarantee of determinism, without which a value stored under that key could never be reliably retrieved again
The second call always returns a value one greater than the first
The function only works correctly the first time it's called
logic_mcq.explanation: Per the lesson's explicit demonstration (`simpleHash('apple', 10)` called twice both returning 3), determinism guarantees identical output for identical input every single time — this is what makes reliable storage and retrieval possible.

logic_mcq.question: Why does the lesson use the prime number 31 as a multiplier in the hash function, rather than 32?
options: 31 and 32 would produce identical results, so it doesn't matter

Power-of-2 multipliers like 32 cause periodic patterns in the lower bits of the resulting hash, leading to clustering; prime multipliers like 31 break this periodicity, spreading hash values more uniformly and reducing collisions
32 is computationally more expensive to multiply by than 31
31 is simply a randomly chosen number with no mathematical justification
logic_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit explanation: 'Using 31 (prime) spreads bits more uniformly than 32 (power of 2). Power-of-2 multipliers cause periodic patterns in lower bits. Primes break periodicity — better distribution, fewer collisions.'

logic_mcq.question: An array has size 1000, and 500 items are inserted with a UNIFORM hash distribution. Per the lesson's reasoning, what's the expected average number of items per slot, and what does this imply about average lookup time?
options: Expected items per slot: 500, implying O(n) lookups
Expected items per slot: 0.5 (500 items / 1000 slots), implying an average lookup requires checking roughly 0.5 items — effectively O(1)
Expected items per slot: 1000, meaning lookups are always slow
This scenario cannot be analyzed without knowing the specific hash function used
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact stated calculation: 500 items distributed uniformly across 1000 slots gives an expected 0.5 items per slot, meaning an average lookup checks well under 1 item — this is the concrete arithmetic behind the O(1) average-case claim.

syntax_mcq.question: In `hash = (hash * 31 + key.charCodeAt(i)) % arraySize;`, what does `key.charCodeAt(i)` return?
options: The character at position i as a string
The numeric Unicode/ASCII code point of the character at position i in the string key — an integer that can be used in arithmetic operations
The total length of the key string
A boolean indicating whether position i exists
syntax_mcq.explanation: `.charCodeAt(i)` returns the numeric character code (e.g., 'a' returns 97) at the given string position, which is necessary here since the hash computation needs a NUMBER to combine arithmetically with the running hash value, not a character/string.

coding_challenges.title: Build and Stress-Test a Custom Hash Function
coding_challenges.problem_statement: Implement the lesson's polynomial hash function, then write tools to empirically verify its determinism and measure its distribution quality (how evenly it spreads a set of keys across array slots).
requirements: Implement `simpleHashImpl(key, arraySize)` matching the lesson's polynomial rolling hash exactly (multiplier 31, modulo arraySize)
Implement `verifyDeterminism(key, arraySize, trials)` that calls simpleHashImpl `trials` times with the same inputs and returns true only if ALL results are identical

Implement `measureDistribution(keys, arraySize)` that hashes every key in the array and returns an object `{ bucketCounts, maxBucketSize, isReasonablyUniform }` where bucketCounts is an array of length arraySize showing how many keys landed in each slot, maxBucketSize is the largest single-slot count, and isReasonablyUniform is true if maxBucketSize <= Math.ceil(keys.length / arraySize) + 2 (a generous uniformity tolerance)
coding_challenges.complexity_analysis: simpleHashImpl: O(k) where k is key length. verifyDeterminism: O(trials * k). measureDistribution: O(n * k) where n is number of keys, k is average key length — each key is hashed once, O(arraySize) to scan bucketCounts for the max.

hints.text: simpleHashImpl: implement exactly as shown in the lesson — running hash multiplied by 31, plus the char code, modulo arraySize, on every character.
verifyDeterminism: store the first call's result, then compare every subsequent call's result against it.
measureDistribution: increment bucketCounts[hash] for each key, then use Math.max(...bucketCounts) to find the largest single bucket.

lessons.title: Hash Maps — Insert, Lookup, Delete
lessons.objective: Use JavaScript's Map for all hash map operations, know the exact time complexity of each, and understand when to use Map over a plain object.
concepts: JavaScript Map: set, get, has, delete, size
Map vs plain object: key types, insertion order, prototype safety
Insert: O(1) amortized
Lookup: O(1) average
Delete: O(1) average
Iteration: O(n) in insertion order
Load factor and automatic resizing
When to use Map vs object literal
lessons.explanation:
JavaScript's Map is the production hash map. Unlike plain objects:
- Map accepts ANY value as a key (functions, objects, NaN, numbers)
- Map preserves insertion order on iteration
- Map has a clean .size property — no Object.keys(obj).length needed
- Map has no prototype pollution risk — a plain object inherits keys like toString and constructor

Operations:
- map.set(key, value): O(1) amortized — inserts or updates
- map.get(key): O(1) average — retrieves value, undefined if missing
- map.has(key): O(1) average — returns boolean, safe for falsy values
- map.delete(key): O(1) average
- map.size: O(1) — stored as a property
- Iteration: O(n) in insertion order

Load factor = items / capacity. When it exceeds ~0.75, the map resizes to double capacity and rehashes all entries — O(n) for that one operation, O(1) amortized across all inserts.

Use Map when: keys are non-strings, order matters, you need .size, or you iterate frequently. Use plain object for simple string-keyed configs that never iterate.
lessons.analogy: A Map is a perfectly organised filing cabinet where each drawer has a unique label (key) and contains exactly one document (value). Adding a document means creating a new labelled drawer in O(1). Finding a document means reading the label directly — O(1), no searching. Deleting means removing the labelled drawer. The cabinet automatically expands when it gets full, which takes a moment but happens rarely enough that the average cost of adding stays O(1).

visual_explanation.description: Draw a comparison table with rows: 'Key types', 'Insertion order', 'Size property', 'Prototype safety', 'Best use case'. Two columns: Map and Plain Object. Map: any value / yes / map.size / no prototype risk / frequency counting and iteration. Plain Object: string/symbol only / no guarantee / Object.keys(obj).length / risk of toString/constructor collision / simple configs. Highlight the 'Key types' and 'Prototype safety' rows as the most important differences. Below the table draw the frequency counter template: const freq = new Map(); freq.set(x, (freq.get(x) || 0) + 1).

code_example.explanation: The frequency counter (freq.get(c) || 0) + 1 is used in nearly every hash map problem in this module. It initialises missing keys to 0 automatically, avoiding an if-else check. However, if valid counts could be 0 (they cannot in a frequency counter but could in other contexts), use freq.has(c) ? freq.get(c) : 0 to avoid the falsy-value trap.

common_mistakes: Reading map.get(key) as a boolean — map.get('missing') returns undefined which is falsy, but map.get('zero') where the value is 0 also returns 0 which is falsy. Always use map.has(key) when you only need to know if the key exists
Using a plain object and calling .hasOwnProperty() to avoid prototype collisions — this works but is verbose. Use Map from the start for any non-trivial data processing
Iterating a Map while deleting entries — modifying a Map during for...of produces unpredictable results. Collect keys to delete first, then delete in a separate pass

interview_war_story.story: The problem required counting character frequencies. The candidate used a plain object: const freq = {}. They then wrote if (freq[c]) freq[c]++ — which incorrectly skips the update when freq[c] is 0 (not possible for frequency counting, but the interviewer changed the problem to counting net changes where values could be 0 or negative). The candidate's code produced wrong answers. Using a Map and freq.has(c) ? freq.get(c) + 1 : 1 would have avoided the falsy-value trap entirely. The interviewer asked 'Why did you use an object instead of Map?' The candidate had no answer.
interview_war_story.lesson: Map is the correct default for all key-value problems in interviews. Plain objects are for configuration, not algorithms. Knowing map.has(key) vs map.get(key) is the difference between code that handles edge cases and code that silently produces wrong answers.

lessons.interview_relevance: Map operations appear in virtually every hash map interview problem. The frequency counter pattern built with Map is the direct implementation of the character map technique from Module 2. Knowing Map.has() vs Map.get() semantics, insertion-order iteration, and O(1) complexity for all core operations is baseline expected knowledge.

questions.question: A Map stores the key 'score' with value 0. Which code correctly checks if the key exists?
options: if (map.get('score')) — truthy check
if (map.has('score')) — existence check that works for any value including 0, false, null
if ('score' in map) — property check
if (map['score'] !== undefined) — undefined check
questions.explanation: map.get('score') returns 0, which is falsy, so if (map.get('score')) would incorrectly evaluate to false even though the key exists. map.has('score') returns true regardless of the value — it only checks if the key is present. Always use .has() when the value could be falsy (0, false, null, empty string).

questions.question: What is the difference between a JavaScript Map and a plain object {} for use as a frequency counter?
options: There is no difference — both work identically for string keys

Map accepts any key type, has no prototype collision risk, has a clean .size property, and guarantees insertion order. Plain objects risk collisions with inherited keys like 'toString' and require Object.keys().length for size.
Plain objects are faster than Map for all operations
Map can only store numbers as values
questions.explanation: For string keys in a controlled dataset, both work. But Map is safer: if a dataset contains the key 'constructor' or 'toString', a plain object would overwrite inherited prototype properties, causing bugs. Map has no prototype — every key is a clean insertion. In interviews, always use Map to avoid prototype pollution surprises.

questions.question: You need to count the frequency of each word in a large text. What is the time complexity of building the frequency Map?
options: O(n²) — comparing each word against all others
O(n log n) — sorting required for frequency counting
O(n) — one pass through all n words, each Map operation is O(1) average
O(1) — Map operations are always constant regardless of input
questions.explanation: Building a frequency map requires one pass through all n words. Each map.set() and map.get() call is O(1) average. Total: O(n) × O(1) = O(n). The resulting map uses O(k) space where k is the number of unique words (≤ n).

coding_quest.title: Word Frequency Counter
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement wordCount(sentence) that returns a Map of each word to its frequency (case-insensitive, split on spaces). Then implement topNWords(sentence, n) that returns the n most frequent words as [word, count] pairs sorted by count descending. Ties broken alphabetically. Use only Map — no sorting libraries for the Map building step.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: A common wrong approach uses a plain object and misses the falsy-value edge case. Also, many beginners forget to handle ties in topNWords and only sort by count, producing non-deterministic output when counts are equal.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n log n) time — correct but missing alphabetical tie-breaking and prototype safety

optimal_solution.complexity: wordCount: O(w) where w = word count. topNWords: O(w log w) for sort. Space: O(u) where u = unique words.

test_cases.input: wordCount('the cat sat on the mat the cat').get('the')
test_cases.label: 'the' appears 3 times

test_cases.input: wordCount('the cat sat on the mat the cat').get('cat')
test_cases.label: 'cat' appears 2 times

test_cases.input: topNWords('the cat sat on the mat the cat', 1)[0][0]
test_cases.label: Top 1 word is 'the'

hints.text: For wordCount: sentence.toLowerCase().split(' ') gives you an array of lowercase words. Loop through them and use freq.set(word, (freq.get(word) || 0) + 1) to increment the count for each word.

For topNWords: spread the map entries into an array with [...freq.entries()], then sort with a comparator that first compares by count descending (b[1] - a[1]) and breaks ties by alphabetical order (a[0].localeCompare(b[0])). Then slice to n.
Sort comparator: (a, b) => b[1] - a[1] || a[0].localeCompare(b[0]). This sorts by count descending; if counts are equal (result = 0), it falls through to the alphabetical comparison.

lessons.mini_challenge: Implement a function wordCount(sentence) that returns a Map of each word to its frequency in the sentence. Then implement topNWords(sentence, n) that returns the n most frequent words as [word, count] pairs sorted by count descending. Use only Map. State the time complexity of topNWords.

theory_mcq.question: Name three concrete advantages JavaScript's Map has over a plain object as described in this lesson.
options: Maps are always faster at every operation with no exceptions
Map accepts ANY value as a key (not just strings), preserves insertion order on iteration, and has no prototype pollution risk (a plain object inherits keys like toString and constructor)
Maps use less memory than objects in every case
Maps can only store numbers, never strings
theory_mcq.explanation: These are the three explicit advantages the lesson lists: arbitrary key types (functions, objects, NaN, numbers — not just strings), guaranteed insertion-order iteration, and avoiding the prototype pollution risk that plain objects carry from inherited properties.

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson specifically recommend using `.has()` rather than relying on a truthy check of `.get()`'s return value, when checking for key existence?
options: Because .has() is always faster than .get()

Because a stored value could itself be falsy (like 0, '', or false) — using `map.get(key) || 'default'` would incorrectly treat a legitimately-stored falsy value as if the key were missing, while `.has()` correctly distinguishes 'key exists with a falsy value' from 'key doesn't exist'
Because .get() doesn't exist as a method on Map
.has() and .get() are functionally identical with no meaningful difference
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit demonstration: `map.set('score', 0); map.get('score') || 'missing'` incorrectly returns 'missing' because 0 is falsy, even though the key genuinely exists with value 0. `.has()` avoids this entire class of bug by checking existence independently of the stored value's truthiness.

theory_mcq.question: What is 'load factor' in the context of hash maps, and what happens when it exceeds the resize threshold?
options: Load factor refers to CPU usage; nothing happens when it's high

Load factor = items / capacity. When it exceeds approximately 0.75, the map automatically resizes to double its capacity and rehashes ALL existing entries — an O(n) operation for that single resize, but amortized to O(1) per insert across the whole sequence of inserts
Load factor only applies to arrays, not hash maps
Exceeding the load factor threshold causes the map to delete random entries
theory_mcq.explanation: This directly parallels L1-M02's dynamic array resizing concept: load factor (items/capacity) crossing ~0.75 triggers a resize-and-rehash, which is O(n) for that operation but amortizes to O(1) per insert overall — the same amortized analysis principle applied to hash maps.

logic_mcq.question: Trace this sequence: `map.set('alice', 95); map.set('bob', 87); map.set('alice', 98);` then `map.get('alice')`. What is returned, and why?
options: 95, since the first value set is always preserved

98 — calling .set() with a key that already exists UPDATES (overwrites) the previous value rather than creating a duplicate entry, so the most recent .set() call for 'alice' determines its current value
[95, 98], an array containing both historical values
undefined, since setting a key twice causes an error
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit demonstration: 'map.set(\'alice\', 98); // update: overwrites previous value' — .set() on an existing key updates rather than duplicates, so .get('alice') returns the most recently set value, 98.

logic_mcq.question: Given the lesson's iteration example, after `map.set('alice', 98); map.set('score', 0); map.delete('bob'); map.set('dave', 91);`, what order will a `for...of` loop over the map produce, and why?
options: Alphabetical order: dave, alice, score
alice, score, dave — in the order each key was MOST RECENTLY set (insertion order is preserved for the surviving keys, and 'bob' is excluded since it was deleted)
Random order, since Maps don't guarantee iteration order
Reverse insertion order: dave, score, alice
logic_mcq.explanation: Map guarantees insertion-order iteration (a key advantage over plain objects per the lesson). Since 'bob' was deleted, it doesn't appear; the remaining keys iterate in the order they were inserted: alice (first), score (second), dave (third) — matching the lesson's example output.

logic_mcq.question: What is the time complexity of building a frequency map via `charFrequency(s)` for a string of length n, and what is its space complexity in terms of k (number of distinct characters)?
options: O(n²) time, O(n²) space

O(n) time — one pass through the string, with O(1) average-case map operations per character — and O(k) space, since the map stores at most one entry per DISTINCT character, not per character occurrence
O(1) time and space regardless of string length
O(n log n) time due to sorting
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's stated complexity: 'Time: O(n) Space: O(k)' — a single linear pass processes each character once (O(n) time), while the map only grows to the number of DISTINCT characters k (not total characters n), giving O(k) space.

syntax_mcq.question: In `freq.set(c, (freq.get(c) || 0) + 1);`, what does this single line accomplish for the frequency counter pattern?
options: It always sets the count to exactly 1

It looks up the current count for character c (defaulting to 0 if c hasn't been seen before, via the `|| 0` fallback), adds 1 to that count, and stores the updated count back — implementing 'increment, or initialize to 1 if first occurrence' in one expression
It deletes character c from the map
It throws an error if c has never been seen before
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is the canonical frequency-counter idiom: `freq.get(c) || 0` safely handles the 'not yet seen' case (returning 0 as a fallback when get() returns undefined), then `+ 1` increments, and `.set()` stores the new count — all combined into one compact, reusable line.

syntax_mcq.question: What does `for (const [key, value] of map)` do when iterating a JavaScript Map?
options: It throws a syntax error; Maps cannot be iterated this way

It iterates over the Map's entries, destructuring each [key, value] PAIR directly into the named variables key and value for use within the loop body — a standard pattern for iterating Map contents in insertion order
It only iterates over the keys, ignoring values entirely
It iterates in random order
syntax_mcq.explanation: Map's default iterator yields [key, value] pairs in insertion order. Destructuring this directly in the for-of loop header (`const [key, value]`) is the standard, idiomatic way to access both the key and value together during iteration.

lessons.title: Hash Sets
lessons.objective: Use JavaScript's Set for O(1) membership testing, duplicate detection, and intersection/union operations — and know precisely when Set is preferable to Map.
concepts: Set: stores unique values, no associated value per entry
Set operations: add, has, delete, size — all O(1) average
Set vs Array for membership testing: O(1) vs O(n)
Converting between Set and Array: new Set(arr) and [...set]
Set intersection, union, and difference
Seen-set pattern for O(n) duplicate detection
When to use Set vs Map
lessons.explanation:
A Set stores unique values with no duplicates and no associated value per entry. Like Map, it uses a hash table internally, giving O(1) average for add, has, and delete.

The critical advantage over Array: arr.includes(x) is O(n) because it scans linearly, while set.has(x) is O(1) because it hashes directly. This single difference changes duplicate detection from O(n²) to O(n).

The seen-set pattern: iterate once, for each element check set.has(element). If true → duplicate found. If false → add to set. Total: O(n) time, O(n) space.

Use Set when: fast existence checking, deduplication, or set operations.
Use Map when: a value must be associated with each key, or you need frequency counts.

Set operations:
- Union: new Set([...a, ...b])
- Intersection: new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))
- Difference: new Set([...a].filter(x => !b.has(x)))
lessons.analogy: A Set is a bouncer's list. Adding a name means writing it once — duplicates are silently ignored. Checking if someone is on the list takes one instant lookup — O(1). An Array is a queue: to check if someone is in the queue, you walk from the front to the back — O(n). The bouncer's list lets you answer 'is this person here?' instantly regardless of how many people are on it.

visual_explanation.description: Draw two columns. Left: 'Array membership check — arr.includes(x)'. Draw an array [1,3,5,7,9] with a scanning arrow moving from left to right one by one, labelled 'O(n) — scan until found or end'. Right: 'Set membership check — set.has(x)'. Draw a hash table with the same values stored at their hash positions. Show a single arrow going directly to the computed slot, labelled 'O(1) — direct hash jump'. Below both: show the impact at scale — n=1,000,000: Array needs up to 1,000,000 checks; Set needs exactly 1. Then show the seen-set loop with each operation labelled O(1).

code_example.explanation: Intersection uses filter + b.has(x). The filter iterates a.size times, and each b.has() call is O(1), so intersection is O(a.size) total — far better than the O(a×b) brute-force nested loop. This pattern appears directly in LeetCode #349 Intersection of Two Arrays.

common_mistakes: Using arr.includes() inside a loop when a Set would give O(1) — this is one of the most common hidden O(n²) patterns. Any time you search an array inside a loop, ask whether a Set built first would work
Assuming Set equality works for objects — new Set([{a:1},{a:1}]).size is 2, not 1, because the two objects are different references. Sets only deduplicate primitives correctly
Forgetting to convert back to array when you need array operations — Sets do not have .map(), .filter(), .reduce(), or indexing. Use [...set] or Array.from(set) when you need these

interview_war_story.story: The problem was Longest Consecutive Sequence (#128). The candidate immediately said 'sort it, then scan — O(n log n).' The interviewer said 'Can you do it in O(n)?' The candidate thought for 2 minutes. The interviewer hinted: 'What if you built a lookup structure first?' The candidate realised: put all numbers into a Set. Then for each number n, only start counting if n-1 is NOT in the set — this ensures you only count from the beginning of each sequence. Each number is visited at most twice (once in the outer loop, at most once in the inner consecutive scan). Total: O(n). The O(n log n) candidate got a 'mixed' signal. The O(n) candidate got a 'strong hire'.
interview_war_story.lesson: Seen Set is the key insight for Longest Consecutive Sequence. Whenever you see 'can you do it in O(n)?', think: can I precompute a Set for O(1) lookups and replace a search with a direct has() call?

lessons.interview_relevance: Set is the data structure behind O(n) solutions to Contains Duplicate (#217), Longest Consecutive Sequence (#128), and Two Sum. The pattern 'build a Set from the input, then query it in O(1)' is one of the most frequently applied transformations in all of Blind 75.

questions.question: Why is checking membership in a Set O(1) while arr.includes() is O(n)?
options: Sets are sorted and use binary search
Sets use a hash table internally — has(x) computes hash(x) and jumps directly to that slot. arr.includes() must scan every element from start until found.
JavaScript engines optimise Sets specially
Sets can only hold numbers which are faster to compare
questions.explanation: Sets use the same hash table mechanism as Maps. has(x) computes hash(x) % capacity and checks that single slot — O(1). arr.includes(x) has no such mechanism — it compares x against every element in sequence until found or exhausted — O(n). Replacing arr.includes() with set.has() inside a loop is one of the most impactful O(n²) → O(n) optimisations.

questions.question: You have two arrays A and B and need to find all elements that appear in both. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Sort both arrays and use two pointers — O(n log n)
Nested loop — check every element of A against every element of B — O(n²)
Build a Set from A (O(n)), then filter B keeping elements where setA.has(element) — O(n) total
Convert both to strings and compare
questions.explanation: Build setA from array A in O(n). Then iterate B — each setA.has() is O(1). Total: O(n) time, O(n) space. This is the Set intersection pattern. The sort + two-pointer approach is O(n log n) and only works on sorted data. Nested loop is O(n²) — too slow for large inputs.

questions.question: new Set([{a:1}, {a:1}]).size returns 2, not 1. Why?
options: Sets cannot store objects

Set deduplication uses reference equality for objects — the two {a:1} literals are different objects in memory even though they look identical. Only primitives (numbers, strings) are deduplicated by value.
The Set contains a bug
Sets always count object properties separately
questions.explanation: JavaScript's Set (and Map) uses the SameValueZero algorithm for equality. For primitives, this means value equality: 1 === 1, 'a' === 'a'. For objects, this means reference equality: two separate {} are never equal even if they have identical contents. This is why Sets only correctly deduplicate primitive values.

coding_quest.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
coding_quest.problem_statement: Given an unsorted array of integers, find the length of the longest consecutive sequence. Example: [100,4,200,1,3,2] → 4 (sequence 1,2,3,4). Apply the 5-step framework. Write the O(n log n) sorting approach first, then the O(n) Set approach. For the O(n) approach: only start counting a sequence from n if n-1 is NOT in the Set.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The wrong approach is starting a count from EVERY number, including those in the middle of a sequence. Without the 'only start if n-1 is not in the set' check, you process [1,2,3,4] four times — once for each start point 1,2,3,4 — giving O(n²) total inner loop work. The key insight eliminates redundant starts.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n²) in the worst case — starts counting from every element including middle of sequences

optimal_solution.complexity: O(n) time — each number is visited at most twice (outer loop once, inner while at most once). O(n) space for the Set.

hints.text: Build a Set from nums first. Then for each num, check if (num-1) is NOT in the set. If it is not, this num is the start of a new sequence. Only then start counting upward.

if (!numSet.has(num - 1)): then set curNum = num, curLen = 1. While numSet.has(curNum + 1): curNum++, curLen++. Update maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, curLen). This inner while only runs for sequence-start elements — each number is in at most one inner while loop total.
for (const num of numSet) { if (!numSet.has(num - 1)) { let curNum = num, curLen = 1; while (numSet.has(curNum + 1)) { curNum++; curLen++; } maxLen = Math.max(maxLen, curLen); } }

lessons.mini_challenge: Solve Longest Consecutive Sequence (LeetCode #128): given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest consecutive sequence. Solve in O(n) using a Set. For each number n, only start counting a sequence if n-1 is NOT in the Set. Apply the 5-step framework before coding.

theory_mcq.question: What is the fundamental structural difference between a Set and a Map?
options: A Set is just a Map with a different name; they're functionally identical
A Set stores unique VALUES with no associated value per entry (just 'is this present or not'), while a Map stores key-VALUE pairs where each key is associated with a separate value
A Set can only store numbers, while a Map can store any type
A Set is always slower than a Map for every operation
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's core distinction: 'A Set stores unique values with no duplicates and no associated value per entry' — unlike a Map, which associates a separate value with each key, a Set only tracks membership (present or absent).

theory_mcq.question: Why does `set.has(x)` being O(1) versus `arr.includes(x)` being O(n) matter so much for duplicate detection specifically?
options: It doesn't matter; both have the same practical performance

Calling an O(n) membership check (.includes()) inside a loop that runs n times produces O(n²) total work; replacing it with an O(1) check (.has()) inside the same loop reduces the total to O(n) — this single substitution is what converts the duplicate-detection pattern from quadratic to linear
arr.includes(x) is actually faster than set.has(x) in all cases
This distinction only matters for arrays larger than 1 billion elements
theory_mcq.explanation: This directly matches the lesson's explicit framing: 'This single difference changes duplicate detection from O(n²) to O(n)' — the O(n)-per-check cost of .includes() inside an n-iteration loop is exactly what produces the O(n²) in hasDuplicate_slow, while .has()'s O(1) cost inside the same loop shape gives O(n) in hasDuplicate_fast.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `seen.add(1); seen.add(2); seen.add(3); seen.add(2);` then `seen.size`. What value does .size return, and why?
options: 4, since four .add() calls were made

3 — Sets automatically deduplicate, so adding the value 2 a second time has NO effect (it's already present), meaning only 3 distinct values (1, 2, 3) exist in the set regardless of how many times .add() was called
2, since only the last two add calls count
An error is thrown on the duplicate add
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's explicit trace: 'seen.add(2); // duplicate — silently ignored... console.log(seen.size); // 3 — not 4' — Sets silently ignore duplicate additions, so .size reflects only the count of DISTINCT values.

logic_mcq.question: Given `const a = new Set([1,2,3,4]); const b = new Set([3,4,5,6]);`, what does `new Set([...a].filter(x => b.has(x)))` compute, and what is the result?
options: The union of a and b: {1,2,3,4,5,6}

The intersection of a and b: {3,4} — this expression spreads a into an array, filters it to keep only elements that ALSO exist in b (via b.has(x)), then wraps the result back into a Set, keeping only values present in BOTH sets
The difference of a and b: {1,2}
An empty set, since a and b share no elements
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's exact worked example: filtering a's elements to keep only those also present in b produces the INTERSECTION — elements common to both sets. For a={1,2,3,4} and b={3,4,5,6}, the shared elements are {3,4}, exactly as the lesson states.

logic_mcq.question: In `hasDuplicate_slow`, the line `nums.slice(0,i).includes(nums[i])` is called inside a loop where i ranges from 0 to n-1. What is the WORST-CASE total cost across all iterations, and why is it O(n²) rather than O(n)?
options: O(n), since each call is fast on its own
O(n²) — each call to .slice(0,i).includes(...) costs O(i) (proportional to how far into the array we are), and summing i from 0 to n-1 gives a total of roughly n²/2, which simplifies to O(n²) overall
O(1), since slice and includes are both constant-time operations
O(log n), since includes uses binary search internally
logic_mcq.explanation: Each iteration's slice+includes cost grows with i (the current position), and summing these costs (0+1+2+...+(n-1)) gives a triangular number proportional to n², matching the lesson's stated 'Total: O(n²)' for this approach, in contrast to the O(n) Set-based alternative.

syntax_mcq.question: What does the spread syntax `[...a, ...b]` do when `a` and `b` are both Sets, in the context of `new Set([...a, ...b])`?
options: It creates a nested array containing two Set objects

It expands (spreads) the elements of both Set a and Set b into a single flat array, which is then passed to `new Set(...)` to construct a new Set containing all the unique elements from both — effectively computing the UNION
It deletes all elements from both sets
It only works if a and b are arrays, not Sets
syntax_mcq.explanation: Spread syntax works on any iterable, including Sets. `[...a, ...b]` produces a single array containing all of a's elements followed by all of b's elements (with possible duplicates across the two), and wrapping this in `new Set(...)` automatically deduplicates, yielding the union.

lessons.title: Collision Handling — Chaining And Open Addressing
lessons.objective: Explain how hash maps handle two keys landing on the same index, and understand why this knowledge affects how you reason about worst-case complexity in interviews.
concepts: Collision definition: two different keys produce the same array index
Separate chaining: each bucket holds a linked list or array
Open addressing: probe for the next empty slot
Linear probing and the primary clustering problem
Quadratic probing and double hashing
Load factor: items / capacity
Resize threshold (~0.75) and rehashing cost
Why worst case is O(n) and when it matters
lessons.explanation:
A collision occurs when two different keys produce the same array index after hashing. Collisions are inevitable for any hash table storing more keys than it has slots — by the pigeonhole principle.

Separate chaining: each slot holds a linked list (or dynamic array). Colliding keys are appended to that slot's list. Lookup hashes to the slot, then scans the list — O(1) average when chains are short, O(n) worst case if all keys collide.

Open addressing: all entries live in the array itself. On collision, probe for the next empty slot.
- Linear probing: check slot+1, slot+2, slot+3 — simple but causes primary clustering
- Quadratic probing: check slot+1², slot+2² — reduces clustering
- Double hashing: uses a second hash function for step size — best distribution

Load factor = items / capacity. Both strategies degrade as the table fills. JavaScript's V8 engine uses open addressing with quadratic probing. Maps resize when load factor exceeds ~0.75, rehashing all entries into the new larger array at O(n) cost.
lessons.analogy: Separate chaining is a hotel where each room can hold multiple guests by adding beds. Two guests getting the same room — they share it. Finding a specific guest means going to their room number and checking each bed. Open addressing is a hotel with exactly one bed per room. A collision means the guest walks down the corridor until finding an empty room. Primary clustering is a long stretch of occupied rooms where guests must walk far to find a free one.

visual_explanation.description: Draw two diagrams side by side. Left: 'Separate Chaining'. Show a hash array of 5 slots. Slot 2 has a linked list with values A → C → E (all hashed to slot 2). Other slots have single values or are empty. Label: 'Collision handled by extending the chain'. Right: 'Open Addressing (Linear Probing)'. Show a hash array of 5 slots. Slot 2 has value A. B tries to go to slot 2 (collision) → probes slot 3 (empty) → placed there. C tries slot 2 (occupied) → slot 3 (occupied) → slot 4 (empty) → placed there. Show the growing cluster with a warning label: 'Primary clustering — long runs slow future insertions and lookups'.

code_example.explanation: The _resize() method is the key — it doubles capacity and rehashes all existing entries. This is the O(n) operation that happens rarely enough to give amortized O(1) insert. Without it, a table that fills to 100% load would have O(n) average lookups due to long chains.

common_mistakes: Treating O(1) map complexity as an absolute guarantee — adversarial inputs that force all keys to one bucket are a real attack vector (hash flooding). Production systems use randomised hash seeds to prevent this

Not knowing the difference between chaining and open addressing when asked — being able to describe both and state their trade-offs (chaining handles high load gracefully; open addressing has better cache locality) is a common senior interview question
Ignoring resize cost — when a map rehashes, every existing entry is recomputed and moved. In latency-sensitive systems this O(n) spike is a real concern even though amortized cost is O(1)

interview_war_story.context: System design round at a Series B startup, 2024
interview_war_story.story: The candidate was designing a caching layer. They said 'We will use a hash map for O(1) lookups.' The interviewer asked 'What happens if an attacker sends requests with keys that all hash to the same bucket?' The candidate froze. The correct answer: 'Hash flooding — all lookups become O(n). Production systems defend against this with randomised hash seeds (SipHash in Python, random seed in Java and Go). In our cache, we should also use a bounded load factor and monitor the distribution of entries per bucket. If we detect clustering, we can rehash with a new seed.' The candidate who knew this got the senior role. The candidate who only knew 'O(1) lookup' got the junior role.
interview_war_story.lesson: In system design interviews, O(1) average is never the final word. Interviewers at senior level always probe worst-case behaviour and adversarial inputs. Knowing about hash flooding and randomised seeds is a senior-level differentiator.

lessons.interview_relevance: System design and senior interviews explicitly ask 'How does a hash map handle collisions?' and 'What is the worst-case complexity and when does it occur?'. Being able to describe both strategies, explain load factor, and discuss hash flooding demonstrates depth beyond basic usage.

questions.question: In separate chaining, what happens when two keys hash to the same index?
options: One key overwrites the other
An error is thrown
Both key-value pairs are stored in a linked list (or array) at that index. Lookup scans the list to find the matching key.
The second key is stored at the next available index
questions.explanation: Separate chaining stores all colliding entries in a list at the same bucket. Each bucket is a linked list or dynamic array. Lookup hashes to the bucket, then linearly scans the list comparing keys. When chains are short (low load factor), this is effectively O(1). Long chains degrade to O(n).

questions.question: A hash map using linear probing becomes 95% full. Why are lookups now slow even for keys that do not collide?
options: Linear probing always takes O(n) regardless of load
At 95% load, primary clustering creates long runs of occupied consecutive slots. Even a non-colliding key may probe through a long cluster of already-occupied slots before finding an empty one.
95% full means 5% of lookups fail
The hash function stops working above 90% load
questions.explanation: Primary clustering: consecutive occupied slots form 'clusters'. A new insertion that lands anywhere in the cluster extends it. At 95% load, these clusters can span dozens of slots. Even a key that would normally hash to an empty area may land at the edge of a large cluster and have to probe through it. Lookup degrades from O(1) to O(cluster length) which can approach O(n).

questions.question: At what load factor do most hash map implementations trigger a resize, and why that specific value?
options: At 100% — only resize when completely full
At 50% — keep the table half empty at all times
At approximately 75% — balances memory efficiency (not too wasteful) with lookup performance (short chains before they get too long)
At 10% — resize early to guarantee O(1)
questions.explanation: 0.75 (75%) is a carefully chosen balance. Below 0.75: average chain length is under 1, guaranteeing very fast lookups. Above 0.75: chains grow quickly and performance degrades noticeably. Resizing at 50% wastes too much memory. Waiting until 100% produces very long chains. 0.75 is the empirically validated sweet spot for most use cases.

coding_quest.title: Implement Hash Map With Chaining And Resize
coding_quest.problem_statement: Implement a HashMap class using separate chaining. wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The most common wrong resize implementation forgets to reset count to 0 before re-inserting. Since set() increments count, and all old entries are being re-inserted, starting count at the old value would double-count all entries and trigger another resize prematurely.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: Logically incorrect — count becomes 2× actual size, causing an immediate second unnecessary resize

optimal_solution.complexity: set: O(1) amortized. get: O(1) average. _resize: O(n) — happens when load > 0.75, amortized O(1) per insert.

For _resize(): save this.buckets to a variable. Double this.capacity. Reset this.buckets to a new array of empty arrays. CRITICAL: set this.count = 0. Then loop through all old buckets and all entries within, calling this.set(k, v) for each.

theory_mcq.question: What is a 'collision' in the context of hash maps, and what is 'separate chaining' as a solution?
options: A collision is a hash function error; chaining fixes the function itself

A collision occurs when two DIFFERENT keys produce the SAME array index. Separate chaining handles this by having each bucket (array slot) hold a small list (or linked list) of all key-value pairs that hashed to that index, rather than just a single value
Collisions never actually occur with modern hash functions
Chaining means deleting one of the two colliding keys automatically
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson defines collision precisely: 'two different keys produce the same array index.' Separate chaining is one resolution strategy — each bucket holds a collection (the lesson's implementation uses an array) of all entries that hash to that index, searched linearly within the (typically small) bucket when needed.

theory_mcq.question: According to the lesson's load factor analysis, what happens to average chain length (and therefore lookup speed) as load factor increases from 0.75 to 5.0?
options: Average chain length stays exactly the same regardless of load factor

Average chain length scales roughly proportionally with load factor — at load 0.75 it's about 0.75 (fast), but at load 5.0 it's about 5 (effectively O(n)-like degraded performance), since load factor directly approximates the expected number of entries sharing a bucket
Average chain length always equals exactly 1, regardless of load factor
Higher load factor always makes lookups faster
theory_mcq.explanation: This matches the lesson's explicit table: 'At load 0.75: avg chain length ≈ 0.75 → fast lookups... At load 5.0: avg chain length = 5 → effectively O(n)' — load factor directly approximates average chain length, which is why resizing before load factor grows too large preserves near-O(1) performance.

logic_mcq.question: Trace the lesson's load factor demonstration: `HashMapChaining(4)` then `set('a',1); set('b',2); set('c',3);`. At what point does a resize get triggered, and why?
options: After set('a',1), since the map starts resizing immediately

After set('c',3) — at that point count=3 and size=4, giving a load factor of 3/4=0.75, which meets the resize threshold (> 0.75 is the trigger condition stated... so this is the boundary case where 0.75 itself may or may not trigger depending on the strict inequality used)
Never, since count never exceeds size
After every single .set() call regardless of count
logic_mcq.explanation: Per the lesson's code, the resize check is `this.count / this.size > 0.75` (strict greater-than). After the third set() call, count=3, size=4, giving exactly 3/4=0.75, which does NOT satisfy the strict `> 0.75` condition — so the resize actually triggers on the FOURTH set() call (count=4, size=4, load=1.0), not the third. This question tests careful reading of the strict inequality.

logic_mcq.question: In the HashMapChaining class, `_resize()` calls `this.set(k, v)` for every existing entry to rebuild the map at the new larger size. Why is this rehashing step necessary, rather than just copying entries directly to a larger array?
options: It's not actually necessary; direct copying would work fine

Because the hash function's output depends on `this.size` (via the modulo operation in `_hash`), so an entry's correct bucket index CHANGES when the array size changes — re-running .set() recomputes each entry's hash against the NEW size, placing it in its correct bucket for the new capacity
Rehashing is only needed for string keys, not numeric keys
Because the resize operation needs to delete half of the existing entries
logic_mcq.explanation: Since `_hash(key)` computes `... % this.size`, the resulting bucket index depends directly on the current size. When size doubles, an entry's correct bucket index is generally different than it was at the old size — simply copying entries to corresponding positions in a larger array would place most entries in the WRONG bucket, hence the need to fully rehash via .set() on each entry.

syntax_mcq.question: In `const existing = bucket.find(([k]) => k === key);`, what does the destructuring `([k]) => k === key` accomplish, given that `bucket` is an array of `[key, value]` pairs?
options: It searches for an exact match of the entire [key, value] pair

For each [key, value] pair in the bucket, it destructures just the first element (the key) into the variable `k`, then checks if `k` matches the target `key` — effectively finding the entry whose KEY matches, ignoring the associated value during the search
It always returns the first element in the bucket regardless of its key
It throws an error if bucket is empty
syntax_mcq.explanation: Each bucket entry is a `[key, value]` pair (array). The arrow function parameter `([k])` destructures just the first element of each pair into `k`, so the `.find()` call searches specifically for an entry whose key matches the target, without needing to separately extract `pair[0]` inside the function body.

lessons.title: Two Sum And Variants
lessons.objective: Solve Two Sum and its four main variants using a hash map, and generalise the single-pass complement-lookup pattern to any pair-finding problem.
concepts: Two Sum: complement lookup in a single pass
Two Sum II: sorted array — two pointers vs hash map trade-off
Three Sum: sort + two pointers + deduplication
Four Sum: generalisation pattern with two outer loops
Two Sum — count pairs: frequency map variant
The complement pattern: complement = target - current
Why hash map beats sorting for unsorted input
Deduplication with skipping in k-sum problems
lessons.explanation:
Two Sum is the canonical hash map problem and the most common entry-level interview question.

Naive: check every pair — O(n²). Hash map: iterate once, for each element compute complement = target - current. Check if complement is already in the map. If yes: found — return indices. If no: store current value → current index in the map.

This single pass is O(n) time, O(n) space. The insight: instead of asking 'does any previous element pair with me?', we ask 'have I already seen what would pair with me?'

Three Sum: sort in O(n log n), then for each element use two pointers on the remaining sorted subarray to find pairs summing to the negative of that element. Deduplication (skipping repeated elements at each pointer) prevents counting the same triplet multiple times. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space.

Key trade-off: for unsorted input, hash map gives O(n). For already-sorted input, two pointers gives O(n) with O(1) space (no map needed). Always check if the input has structure before choosing a strategy.
lessons.analogy: Two Sum with a hash map is like finding two puzzle pieces that fit together. Instead of trying every piece against every other piece (O(n²)), you describe the shape you need (the complement) and check a lookup box of shapes you have already seen (the hash map). If the shape is in the box, you found your pair instantly. You only walk through the pile once.

visual_explanation.description: Draw array [2, 7, 11, 15] with target=9. Show the hash map (seen) as a box that grows as we scan. Step 1: i=0, num=2, complement=9-2=7, seen={}. Is 7 in seen? No. Add 2→0 to seen. Step 2: i=1, num=7, complement=9-7=2, seen={2:0}. Is 2 in seen? YES! Return [seen.get(2), 1] = [0, 1]. Draw each step as a row with: current number, complement being checked, contents of seen map, and result. Annotate: 'We found 7 looking for 2, which was already recorded at index 0.' Compare to brute force: 2×2=4 pairs checked total in brute force vs 2 iterations in hash map.

code_example.explanation: Three Sum's deduplication (skip when nums[i] === nums[i-1]) is critical and the most common place to introduce bugs. The guard i > 0 prevents out-of-bounds at i=0. Without deduplication, [-1,-1,0,1] would produce [[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1]] — the same triplet twice, which is a wrong answer.

common_mistakes: Storing the value without the index in the Two Sum map — the problem asks for indices, so the map must store value→index. Storing value→boolean gives you that a pair exists but not where
Not handling duplicates in Three Sum — failing to skip repeated values for the outer loop and both pointers produces duplicate triplets. The guard i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i-1] is mandatory
Using a hash map on Two Sum II (sorted input) — when the array is already sorted, two pointers gives O(n) time and O(1) space, strictly better than a hash map's O(n) space

interview_war_story.story: The first problem was Two Sum. The candidate wrote a nested loop — O(n²). The OA system ran 25 test cases including n=100,000 arrays. 23 cases timed out. The candidate was eliminated. The O(n) hash map solution passes all 25 cases in milliseconds. The algorithm is 4 lines: create a map, loop once, check complement, add to map. Every candidate preparing for Amazon's OA must be able to write those 4 lines from memory in under 2 minutes, with the correct time and space complexity stated.
interview_war_story.lesson: Two Sum is not a problem to 'figure out' in an interview. It is a pattern to have memorised cold: complement = target - num, check seen map, add to seen map. The 4 lines take under 2 minutes. An O(n²) Two Sum is an automatic elimination at every company that tests it.

lessons.interview_relevance: Two Sum (#1) appears in virtually every junior interview. Three Sum (#15) is Blind 75 and consistently appears at mid-level interviews. Being able to solve both fluently, explain the hash map vs two-pointer trade-off, and handle duplicates in Three Sum is a clear competency signal.

questions.question: In Two Sum using a hash map, you iterate through nums and for each element check if (target - nums[i]) is in the seen map. Why do you check BEFORE adding nums[i] to the map?
options: Order does not matter — checking before or after gives the same result
Checking before ensures you do not use the same element twice. If you added first, then an element could pair with itself (e.g., [3,5] target=6 would incorrectly pair 3 with itself).
Adding first would overwrite previous entries
The map only accepts one entry at a time
questions.explanation: If we add first then check, an element at index i could match its own complement if target = 2 × nums[i]. For example: [3,5], target=6. If we add 3 first, then check complement 6-3=3, we find it immediately and return [0,0] — using index 0 twice. The problem requires two DIFFERENT indices. Checking before adding prevents self-pairing.

questions.question: Three Sum returns all unique triplets summing to 0. After sorting and finding a valid triplet [a,b,c], what must you do next to avoid duplicates?
options: Start over from the beginning
Skip all elements equal to the current left and right pointers before moving them, to avoid generating the same triplet from different starting positions
Remove the found triplet from the array
Sort the result and remove duplicates at the end
questions.explanation: After finding [a,b,c] at positions left/right: advance left pointer while nums[left] === nums[left+1], and retreat right while nums[right] === nums[right-1]. This skips all duplicates of the current left and right values before moving the pointers. Without this, [-1,-1,0,1,1] would produce [[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1]] — the same triplet twice.

questions.question: Two Sum on an unsorted array: hash map (O(n) time, O(n) space) vs sort+two-pointers (O(n log n) time, O(1) space). Which should you choose and why?
options: Always use the hash map — it is faster
Always use sort+two-pointers — it uses less memory

Hash map when memory is available and O(n) time matters most. Sort+two-pointers when memory is constrained and O(n log n) time is acceptable. For unindexed problems (just return whether a pair exists), sort+two-pointers saves space.
They are equivalent — choose either
questions.explanation: It depends on constraints. Hash map: O(n) time (faster), O(n) space (more memory). Sort+two-pointers: O(n log n) time (slower), O(1) space (no extra memory, only valid when you do not need to sort a copy). The Two Sum problem asks for INDICES, so you must not reorder the array — hash map is the correct choice. If the problem only asked 'does a pair exist?', you could sort in-place and use two pointers.

wrong_approach_shown_first.explanation: The wrong approach adds nums[i] to the map BEFORE checking for the complement. This allows an element to pair with itself. Example: [3,5] target=6. Adding 3 first, then checking complement 3 — found at index 0! Returns [0,0] — wrong, same element used twice. Check complement FIRST, then add.
wrong_approach_shown_first.naive_complexity: O(n) time but logically incorrect — can return [i, i] using the same element twice

The order is: CHECK complement first, then ADD current element. This prevents self-pairing where an element matches its own complement. Example: [3,5] target=6 — checking complement 3 before adding 3 ensures index 0 (3) is not in seen yet when we check for 3.
if (seen.has(complement)) return [seen.get(complement), i]; seen.set(nums[i], i);

theory_mcq.question: Why does the lesson recommend hash map for UNSORTED Two Sum but two pointers for SORTED Two Sum, when both achieve O(n) time?
options: There's no real reason; either approach works equally well in all cases

Both achieve O(n) time, but the hash map approach uses O(n) extra space while the two-pointer approach (only possible when input is already sorted) uses O(1) extra space — since two pointers is strictly better on space with the same time complexity, it should be preferred whenever the input is already sorted
Hash map is always faster than two pointers regardless of input
Two pointers cannot be used on unsorted arrays under any circumstances, which is the only reason
theory_mcq.explanation: The lesson's explicit comparison: 'Unsorted input -> hash map (O(n) time, O(n) space). Sorted input -> two pointers (O(n) time, O(1) space) <- strictly better.' When both achieve the same time complexity, the lower-space option is preferable, which is only available when the input happens to already be sorted.

theory_mcq.question: In `threeSum`, why is deduplication ('skip outer duplicates' and the two inner while-loop skips) necessary, given the problem asks for UNIQUE triples?
options: Deduplication is unnecessary; the problem doesn't actually require unique triples

Since the array contains possible duplicate VALUES, naively iterating over every index combination could produce the SAME triple of values multiple times (just at different index combinations) — explicit duplicate-skipping logic at each pointer level ensures each distinct VALUE COMBINATION is only added to the result once
Deduplication is only needed if the array has more than 1000 elements
Deduplication removes negative numbers from the result
theory_mcq.explanation: Without explicit skip-logic, a sorted array with repeated values (e.g., [-1,-1,0,1,1]) could produce the same valid triple of VALUES from multiple different index combinations, violating the 'unique triples' requirement — the lesson's skip-while-loops specifically prevent revisiting the same value at each pointer position after it's already been used to form a result.

logic_mcq.question: Trace `twoSum([2,7,11,15], target=9)` per the lesson's own trace. At i=0, what happens? At i=1, what happens?
options: At i=0: complement=7, found in seen, returns immediately. At i=1: never reached.
At i=0: complement=9-2=7, NOT yet in seen (seen is empty), so add {2:0} to seen. At i=1: complement=9-7=2, WHICH IS in seen (at index 0), so return [0, 1]
At i=0: complement=2, found immediately. At i=1: the function has already terminated.
The function never finds a valid pair for this input.
logic_mcq.explanation: This is the lesson's own explicit trace: 'i=0: complement=7, not in seen -> add {2:0}. i=1: complement=2, IN SEEN at 0 -> return [0,1]' — confirming the single-pass complement-lookup mechanism step by step.

logic_mcq.question: Why does `twoSumSorted` return `[left + 1, right + 1]` (adding 1 to each index) rather than just `[left, right]`?
options: This is a bug; it should return [left, right] directly

This specific variant of Two Sum (Two Sum II) is defined to use 1-INDEXED positions in its expected output (a convention specified by this particular problem, distinct from the standard 0-indexed Two Sum), so the function adds 1 to convert from JavaScript's 0-indexed array positions to the expected 1-indexed answer format
Adding 1 doubles the search space
This only works correctly for arrays with an even number of elements
logic_mcq.explanation: This reflects a real, problem-specific convention: 'Two Sum II' (a specific, named variant) is commonly specified to return 1-indexed positions rather than the standard 0-indexed positions used elsewhere — the +1 adjustment converts the 0-indexed `left`/`right` pointer positions to match this expected output format.

logic_mcq.question: What is the time complexity of `threeSum` as implemented, and what determines this complexity (rather than O(n) like the basic two-pointer Two Sum)?
options: O(n), identical to basic Two Sum

O(n²) — the OUTER loop runs O(n) times (once per potential first element of the triple), and for EACH outer iteration, the inner two-pointer scan does up to O(n) work, giving O(n) × O(n) = O(n²) total, on top of the O(n log n) initial sort which is dominated by the O(n²) term
O(n³), since three numbers must be checked
O(log n), since the array is sorted first
logic_mcq.explanation: Matching the lesson's stated complexity 'O(n²) time, O(1) space' — the structure is an O(n) outer loop wrapping an O(n) two-pointer inner scan, giving O(n²) total, which dominates the one-time O(n log n) sort cost at the start.

syntax_mcq.question: In `if (i > 0 && nums[i] === nums[i-1]) continue;`, what does this line accomplish within threeSum's outer loop?
options: It skips the very first element of the array unconditionally

It skips the current outer-loop iteration if the current element is a DUPLICATE of the PREVIOUS element (and we're not at index 0) — preventing the same value from being used as the 'first element' of a triple more than once, which would otherwise produce duplicate triples in the result
It sorts the array in descending order
It terminates the entire function early
syntax_mcq.explanation: This is the outer-loop deduplication check: since the array is sorted, identical consecutive values sit next to each other — checking `nums[i] === nums[i-1]` (with the `i > 0` guard to avoid an out-of-bounds check at index 0) skips redundant starting points that would otherwise generate duplicate triples.
